meta.title: Account takeover through MFA push fatigue
meta.tagline: How one approved prompt became mailbox forwarding and file access, and how it was closed.
meta.redaction: User, analysts and on-call named by role only. Source address shown as a hosting provider, not an IP. External forwarding address and file names omitted. No passwords or tokens appear.

source.ref: grouping of events by what the attacker needed

steps.title: Fake sign-in page takes password
steps.body: A phishing email sends the finance user to a fake single sign-on page. The user enters a password there, and the attacker signs in with it from a hosting provider.

steps.title: Repeated pushes until one is approved
steps.body: The identity provider sends push after push to the user. Most are denied, then the user approves one to make the prompts stop.

steps.title: A medium-risk session is issued
steps.body: The provider issues a session to an unknown device. It rates the risk medium and does not block it, so the attacker is in.

steps.title: Forwarding rule and a rogue app
steps.body: The attacker adds a rule forwarding invoices to an outside address. They also consent to an unverified app that can read mail and all files.

steps.title: Finance files are opened
steps.body: Files in the finance share are opened while the session is live. The record does not say how many were downloaded.

steps.title: The user reports, responders revoke
steps.body: The user reports the prompt soon after approving it. Responders confirm the push spam in the logs, then revoke sessions, reset the password and remove the app consent.

steps.title: Where the chain could be cut
steps.body: These settings sit where the attacker got through. They are illustrative, not findings from the incident record.

controls.name: Block medium-risk sessions
controls.why: The session was issued at medium risk and was not blocked.

source.ref: suggested from IdP log 09:13:06 risk=medium; not stated by the owner

controls.name: Block unverified app consent
controls.why: The consent was granted to an app with an unverified publisher.

source.ref: suggested from IdP log 09:22:41 publisher=unverified; not stated by the owner

events.note: An email with a link to a fake sign-in page reaches the finance user.
The user types their password into the fake page.
The password works from a hosting provider address on an unknown device.
Pushes reach the user and are denied.

source.ref: IdP log 08:52:03 to 09:12:40, denied x22; channel 09:31

events.note: The user approves a prompt they did not start.
A session is issued to an unknown device at medium risk and is not blocked.
The user tells on-call about a login prompt they did not start.
A rule forwards invoices to an external address.
An unverified app receives mail and file read scopes.
Files are opened in the finance share; downloads are not known.
Analysts confirm the push requests in the identity logs.

events.action: password reset and app consent removed
events.note: The password is reset and the app consent is taken away.

_gaps: Who opened the 41 files (attacker session or the app) is not stated; the app-to-share link is illustrative.
Whether the 09:13:05 approval is the 23rd push or a 24th is unclear; 22 denied plus 1 approved matches the 23 in the channel.
Why a medium-risk session was not blocked (policy) is not stated.
Whether the forwarded invoices were actually delivered externally is not stated.
